chat.author: Suresh Krishnan
chat.text: https://github.com/ietf-wg-aipref/drafts/pull/260

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: The pull request is pretty long, necessarily.  Kevin's slides are going to be a far better reference for what it seeks to achieve.

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: Small terminology point: RFC 9309's abstract describes robots.txt as controlling whether content 'may be accessed, if at all' by crawlers. That's a consent signal about acquisition, not traffic management. I'd rather the drafts use the RFC's framing.

chat.author: Ted Hardie
chat.text: How is this meant to work when the _usage_train-ai rule is different for different User Agents?

chat.author: Ted Hardie
chat.text: Overloading User-agent seems to prevent that, which may be awkward.

chat.author: Suresh Krishnan
chat.text: @Mark, are you concerned about specific text in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-aipref-attach-05

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: At this level, this is pretty much just a change in spelling.  If we were to get precious about spelling, ...

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: @Suresh Krishnan No, attach-05 is fine. The phrase is in draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal §1 and §4.3 and the slides ('traffic management signals'). If that framing moves into the WG drafts via #260, I'd like it to follow RFC 9309's 'may be accessed, if at all' instead.

chat.author: Chris Needham
chat.text: I had a similar question to Ted. I'm not sure how a website would selectively allow AI usage on particular paths

chat.author: Suresh Krishnan
chat.text: Thanks for clarifying Mark.

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text: I don't care about the spelling, but I'm actually not 100% sure this can express everything that one might want to express.

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: +1 Ted. And if the answer is vendor-specific tokens, per-vendor consent ends up defined in each vendor's documentation rather than in the WG's vocabulary.

chat.author: Jon Geater
chat.text: What about "text yes but images no?"

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: it would also seem to suggest that if anything new came up in the future, it would also have to be stuffed into the User-Agent string, forever

chat.author: Ted Hardie
chat.text: @Chris this seems to indicate that cross-vendor behaviour uses the usage_train-ai User Agent, but otherwise you use Content-Usaage.

chat.author: Chris Needham
chat.text: I think the answer is per vendor tokens, what Kevin's calling proprietary policy tokens?

chat.author: Rich Salz
chat.text: It's the TXT entry for robots

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
Eric Rescorla said:

I don't care about the spelling, but I'm actually not 100% sure this can express everything that one might want to express.

I think that this can express everything that the current draft does.

chat.author: Ted Hardie
chat.text: But I have not read the PR, just trying to follow the slides.

chat.author: Thom Vaughan
chat.text: :pinched_fingers:

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: @Ted Hardie as I read #260's diff it removes the robots.txt Content-Usage rule entirely (only the HTTP header stays). So per-vendor differences would rely on proprietary tokens.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: You need to read the REP namespaces draft to understand this.  And that draft is, sadly, hard to read.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: As I said before, Kevin's slides are the best reference you can use to understand this.

chat.author: Daniel Gillmor
chat.text: what if my browser's user-agent is "__dkg"

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: I believe that Kevin checked for "__" in robots.txt files and found none.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: I don't believe that it is necessary to reserve anything other than the prefix.

chat.author: Daniel Gillmor
chat.text: it seems like the question is more about whether any user-agent string has __ in it, though, right?  not just about whether any robots.txt includes it.

chat.author: Daniel Gillmor
chat.text: but also, i'm actually fine with saying "don't include __ in your user-agent string"

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Yes, that's true, but if no one is targeting those user agents, does it matter?

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Trees, forest, etc...

chat.author: Philippe Dellaert
chat.text: Begins with, right, not include?

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Right now, Kevin is proposing to reserve the __ sequence anywhere in the label.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: I'm suggesting that maybe we can just reserve the prefix.

chat.author: Philippe Dellaert
chat.text: Ah, thanks for the clarification. I think reserving the prefix is the right way if we want to take this forward

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text: I think that previous slide ought to give you pause about this design

chat.author: Rohan Mahy
chat.text:
as an outsider watching this presentation, robots.txt seems like an insufficient grammar for expressing the examples described in this presentation. 
My mind is wandering to the warning in a famous post about using regex to parse HTML

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: If private agreements override the signal, the spec should say so neutrally, and say the signal is still the site's stated preference. Otherwise 'override' reads as 'the preference is a default you can buy out of'.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
Eric Rescorla said:

I think that previous slide ought to give you pause about this design

Say more?

chat.author: Daniel Gillmor
chat.text:
it seems like the tl;dr here is: robots.txt is a mess and the world is full of inconsistent interpretation.  here's a thing that doesn't make the inconsistencies significantly worse, but increases the complexity. 
I'm don't find that particularly compelling.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
Mark Atwood said:

If private agreements override the signal, the spec should say so neutrally, and say the signal is still the site's stated preference. Otherwise 'override' reads as 'the preference is a default you can buy out of'.

The drafts already say that private agreements can override preferences.

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: policy tokens are a thing that exists, but people kinda dislike them, right? it violates the expectation that it matches what comes in User-Agent headers

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: On slide 15: your no-wildcard-fallback rule is there so no one accidentally expresses a positive preference. The same principle says an unmatched path in a usage group should be 'no preference', as in your initial draft, not train-ai=y. Writing one Disallow shouldn't silently opt every other path in.

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text: I think the real question here is not do robots parsers not behave uniformly but rather "If we do the thing in attachment does it break existing parsers"

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: Spelling out the problems with the current approach would indeed be useful

chat.author: Daniel Gillmor
chat.text: Mirja++

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: I think that the slides were clear on that.

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text:
Martin Thomson said:

I think that the slides were clear on that.

Not clear to me at least

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
It's pretty tricky to understand
User-Agent: *
Content-Usage: train-ai=n

User-Agent: FooBot
Allow: /

chat.author: Erin Simon
chat.text: only until we give conflict resolution rules

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Whether that is two groups or one is non-deterministic.  And we are not able to specify what to do there, because that involves deployed code.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Consider also the option with no blank line.

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: so not only would we have cross-vendor policy tokens, but literally every vendor has to implement policy tokens now?

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Of course, that is well-defined in the current specification.  But that's no consolation when a deployed parser has to handle this consistently.

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: parsers have to adapt in both cases

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: yes, robots.txt has ambiguity. I guess the answer to that is we should fix robots.txt, no?

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: No, the point is that you don't want to cause harm by people deploying preferences to robots.txt files in the sense that they would cause existing parsers to reach different conclusions.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Fixing robots.txt is worthwhile, but it is not going to fix existing parsers.

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text:
Martin Thomson said:

No, the point is that you don't want to cause harm by people deploying preferences to robots.txt files in the sense that they would cause existing parsers to reach different conclusions.

Exactly. So I think we need to evaluate how often that will hapen

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: existing parser already come to different conclusions eventually, no?

chat.author: Thibault Meunier
chat.text: do we know if the discrepancies in parsers are based on interpretation of REP, extensions, others?

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: A parser that is updated is easy.  What we want to do is ensure that someone can update their robots.txt file to express preferences without changing what existing parsers read from that (and subsequently crawl).

chat.author: Eric Rescorla
chat.text:
Martin Thomson said:

A parser that is updated is easy.  What we want to do is ensure that someone can update their robots.txt file to express preferences without changing what existing parsers read from that (and subsequently crawl).

Exactly. I'm not worried about the case where if we sort of extend existing parser behavior to -attach-05, they break things. That's their problem. My concern is with unmodified parsers misbehaving. For instance, I add train-ai=n and it gets interpreted as "nobody can scrape at all" by a lot of existing parsers

chat.author: Ted Hardie
chat.text: Overloading an existing field seems to be a risky move if the aim is to not break parsers, though it does appear Kevin's work to investigate them alleviates that concern a bit.

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: policy tokens instead of actual user-agent tokens creates a lot of confusion, and this would make it worse. it used to be that you saw a crawler, and then applied a policy back the crawler you saw with the same token.

chat.author: Ted Hardie
chat.text: robots.txt seems to be a dancing bear at this point (“The wonder is not that the dancing bear dances well, it is that the bear dances at all.” if the reference is opaque.)

chat.author: Steve Traugott
chat.text: Seems to me that the right path is to let robots.txt remain broken as designed; we're not going to fix all existing parsers.  Then start fresh with a new blob that allows servers/CDNs to better detect and deal with the bad behavior that results from ignoring or misinterpreting the new thing.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Now, my main concern is less about the group splitting (which is clear), but the empty group version.  We might be able to fix each of these problems with stronger guidance to authors of robots.txt documents so that they can avoid the problems.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Nick, that's not how GoogleExtended works.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: I do think that there is a good discussion to have about policy tokens here, but maybe this group doesn't have to be where that discussion happens.

chat.author: Mark Atwood
chat.text: @Steve Traugott Careful with CDN-side enforcement: that turns a preference into a gate. Vocab §3.2 says receivers choose whether to follow preferences; a new format shouldn't quietly change that.

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: MT, I think I understood Google Extended from reading the documentation closely, and the person I was advising misunderstood. but maybe we both misunderstood ;)

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: maybe breaking existing parser is the way to get them fixed...?

chat.author: Rony Shalit
chat.text:
Excuse me for the obvious question, but didn't we agree that robots.txt is broken and should not be used for attachment over a year ago. This was discussed in the first group meetings and over email, with examples of why robots.txt should NOT be used.
Wasn't that part of the split between vocabulary and attachment?

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: My understanding is that Google Extended only governs usage, not crawling.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
Rony Shalit said:

Excuse me for the obvious question, but didn't we agree that robots.txt is broken and should not be used for attachment over a year ago. This was discussed in the first group meetings and over email, with examples of why robots.txt should NOT be used.
Wasn't that part of the split between vocabulary and attachment?

That was not the conclusion.  We wanted to ensure that this was under the noses of crawlers and that robots.txt was the best way to do that.

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: not sure if trying to hack around the limitations of a broken protocol is the way to success, especially if that imposes a lot of complexity. I wondering how far we could get if we better specify parser behavior and do some targeted outreach.

chat.author: Nick Doty
chat.text: Martin, yeah, that's my understanding of Extended as well. but I think that's the source of confusion, that people start looking for it as a User-Agent token, when in fact it's not used there.

chat.author: Mirja Kühlewind
chat.text: (independent of the question how we add the ai preference to robots.txt)
